newsitem.title: USA: Ovitz' departure revives Disney succession issue.
newsitem.headline: Ovitz' departure revives Disney succession issue.

text.p: The sudden departure of Michael Ovitz from Walt Disney Co. has revived questions about who will succeed Chairman Michael Eisner at the giant entertainment company.
Ovitz, the Hollywood powerbroker hired a year ago to help Eisner expand Disney's empire overseas, stepped down on Thursday, ending a rocky tenure since he joined Disney in October 1995.
Industry analysts said the departure of Ovitz, widely regarded as the heir apparent to Eisner, raises new questions about who will lead Disney when Eisner chooses to retire.
"Succession is a key issue,' said Cowen & Co. analyst Harold Vogel.
Disney officials told analysts the firm was likely to look inside the company for someone to succeed Ovitz. But they said Eisner did not appear to be in any hurry to name a successor.
At the top of the list may be Robert Iger, chief executive at ABC, who reportedly has developed a good relationship with Eisner since Disney acquired Capital Cities/ABC Inc.
"If he turns ABC around" he stands a good chance of being promoted, Vogel said, adding "right now ABC is not running in the right direction."

The issue of who would succeed Eisner, 54, has hung over Disney since he underwent quadruple bypass surgery in 1994. When Disney hired Ovitz last year, the company thought the succession issue was finally put to rest. But friction quickly developed between Ovitz and some Disney managers used to running their own show.

For example, he ruffled feathers at ABC when he became involved in hiring former NBC executive Jamie Tarses earlier this year and was rebuffed by Disney studio boss Joe Roth for meddling in movie deals with top Hollywood stars.
Some insiders said Ovitz has had a hard time adjusting to life in a corporation where he is not the ultimate deal maker.
"Michael Ovitz was a very effective talent agent but it's a lot harder to run a big company like Disney," said one industry executive.

Ovitz, who co-founded the powerful talent firm Creative Artists Agency, has not decided what he will do next, but regardless will be well compensated. According to people familar with his termination agreement, Ovitz stands to pocket an estimated $90 million in cash and stock options.

Ovitz, 49, is not the first executive to leave Disney in recent years. Jeffrey Katzenberg stormed out of Disney's executive offices in 1994 after Eisner refused to name him president after the death of Eisner's trusted friend Frank Wells in a helicopter crash.

Katzenberg is currently seeking more than $250 million from Disney for money he claims the company owes him for helping revive Disney's animated film unit with blockbusters like "Beauty and the Beast", "Aladdin" and "The Lion King."
Stephen Bollenbach, the architect of Disney's $19 billion acquisition of Capital Cities/ABC, left earlier this year to take the top job at Hilton Hotels Corp.
Disney TV chief Richard Frank left last year after Eisner decided to reorganize the company's operations.
